1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text:
[Case 1] A 67-year-old male patient was admitted with the chief complaint of "cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis for 2 years." He was treated at a local hospital with cefoperazone/sulbactam combined with levofloxacin, with poor therapeutic effect. The patient had a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis, bronchiectasis, hypertension, and other diseases. Chest CT showed a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe, measuring approximately 4.2 cm × 5.8 cm. This patient was admitted with "cavitary lung lesion of unclear etiology."
[Case 2] A 38-year-old female patient was admitted with the chief complaint of "intermittent hemoptysis for 1 year." One year earlier, because of hemoptysis, she underwent bronchoscopy at another hospital and was diagnosed with "Nocardia" infection. She was treated with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 1 year. The patient developed elevated serum creatinine, and the therapeutic effect was poor. Hemoptysis recurred, and she was admitted to our Department of Respiratory Medicine. Chest CT showed bronchiectasis in the bilateral lower lobes, with mucus plugs in some bronchial lumens.
[Case 3] A 35-year-old female patient was admitted with the chief complaint of "intermittent hemoptysis for 4 days." At a local hospital, she was sequentially treated with levofloxacin and hemostatic agents such as Yunnan Baiyao, with poor effect. Chest CT showed cystic bronchiectatic changes in the right lower lobe, with an aspergilloma within the cavity and surrounding exudative opacities.
[Case 4] A 72-year-old male patient was admitted with the chief complaint of "fever accompanied by cough and sputum production for 2 weeks." At a local hospital, he was sequentially treated with cefoperazone/sulbactam, meropenem, doxycycline, and methylprednisolone, with poor therapeutic effect. Chest CT showed consolidative and exudative opacities in both lungs.
[Case 5] A 36-year-old female patient was admitted with the chief complaint of "recurrent cough and sputum production for more than 30 years, worsening for 4 months." Chest CT showed partial bronchiectasis in both lungs with infection.
[Case 6] An 18-year-old male patient was admitted because of "cough, sputum production, and blood-streaked sputum for 2 months." Chest CT showed partial bronchiectasis in both lungs with infection. He had a past history of diabetes mellitus, with extremely poor glycemic control.
[Case 7] A 62-year-old male patient was admitted with the chief complaint of "recurrent cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea for more than 1 year, worsening for 3 days." The patient had poor response after treatment with cephalosporins. Chest CT showed bilateral bronchiectasis with inflammation.
[Case 8] A 56-year-old male patient was admitted with the chief complaint of "recurrent dyspnea for more than 1 year, worsening with fever for more than 1 month." The patient had been on long-term oral glucocorticoid therapy for hypersensitivity pneumonitis. In the month before admission, generalized weakness, fever, and sore throat worsened. Chest CT showed bilateral ground-glass opacities, interlobular septal thickening, and traction bronchiectasis.
[Case 9] An 82-year-old male patient was admitted with the chief complaint of "cough for more than 3 months, worsening with wheezing and dyspnea for more than 1 month." In the 3 months before admission, the patient had been on long-term oral glucocorticoid therapy for ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis, and recently developed worsening dyspnea. Chest CT showed reticular and ground-glass opacities in both lungs, interlobular septal thickening, and traction bronchiectasis.
[Case 10] A 62-year-old male patient was admitted with the chief complaint of "cough and shortness of breath for more than 10 years, worsening with intermittent fever for 2 months." This patient had a clear prior diagnosis of COPD and was currently receiving inhaled budesonide/glycopyrrolate/formoterol. He had been repeatedly hospitalized for COPD and had received intravenous glucocorticoid therapy. Two months earlier, recurrent fever developed, accompanied by joint pain with each episode, with a maximum temperature of 39℃. At a local hospital, intravenous glucocorticoids and antibiotics including cephalosporins led to improvement, but the patient continued to have recurrent fever, occurring approximately once every 10-15 days. Ten days earlier, fever recurred again; cefoperazone/sulbactam and intravenous methylprednisolone relieved the symptoms, but they recurred after discontinuation, and he was admitted for further diagnosis and treatment. Chest CT showed bronchitis, emphysema, pulmonary bullae, and inflammatory lesions in both lungs, more prominent in the right lung.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary aspergillosis spectrum (chronic pulmonary aspergillosis/aspergilloma)
supporting_evidence: Among Case 1 through Case 10, these 10 patients either had underlying bronchiectasis (underlying structural lung damage) or comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus, oral corticosteroid use, COPD, and rheumatoid arthritis; all of these are high-risk factors for fungal infection. Most had cavitary lesions or aspergilloma formation on imaging.
opposing_evidence: The CT findings in Case 8 and Case 9 were "bilateral ground-glass opacities, interlobular septal thickening, and traction bronchiectasis" or "bilateral reticular and ground-glass opacities, interlobular septal thickening, and traction bronchiectasis," which are more suggestive of a diffuse interstitial/alveolar process rather than the typical imaging appearance of chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis.
Not all cases described cavitation or aspergilloma.

differential_diagnoses.name: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis
supporting_evidence: Case 8: A 56-year-old man, on long-term oral glucocorticoid therapy for hypersensitivity pneumonitis, recently developed worsening generalized fatigue, fever, and sore throat. Chest CT showed bilateral ground-glass opacities, interlobular septal thickening, and traction bronchiectasis; the images showed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities and interstitial changes, with an obvious immunosuppressed background.

Case 9: An 82-year-old man, on long-term oral glucocorticoid therapy for ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis, with recent worsening dyspnea. CT showed bilateral reticular and ground-glass opacities, interlobular septal thickening, and traction bronchiectasis, representing a high-risk background for opportunistic infection.

Case 10: A 62-year-old man was repeatedly hospitalized for COPD and was "treated with intravenous glucocorticoids." Over the past 2 months, he had "recurrent fever." Chest CT showed "bilateral inflammatory lesions in both lungs, more pronounced in the right lung," and the condition still recurred after antibacterial therapy.
Case 6: An 18-year-old male, "with a history of diabetes mellitus and very poor glycemic control," has impaired immune defenses, which may increase the risk of invasive fungal infection.
opposing_evidence: Cases 1, 2, and 3 had a relatively long clinical course, characterized mainly by chronic hemoptysis, cavitation, or bronchiectasis, which is more consistent with a chronic/colonizing process rather than a typical acute invasive process.
No more typical high-risk background, such as definite neutropenia, transplantation, or hematologic malignancy, was provided in the first-stage information.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease
supporting_evidence: Case 1: A 67-year-old man with chronic "cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis for 2 years"; CT showed "a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe." An upper lobe cavity with hemoptysis is an important differential diagnostic consideration for TB/mycobacterial disease.

Cases 2, 5, and 7 have bronchiectasis, chronic cough and sputum production, and hemoptysis/chest tightness and dyspnea; chronic airway structural destruction can also be seen in nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease.
In some cases, the response to antibacterial therapy is poor, suggesting that chronic infectious pathogens other than common bacteria should be considered.
opposing_evidence: In case 3, CT showed an "intracavitary aspergilloma," which is more supportive of a fungal lesion.
The diffuse ground-glass opacities and septal thickening in Case 8 and Case 9 are not typical imaging manifestations of cavitary tuberculosis.
The information from the first stage did not provide clear supporting clues such as night sweats, weight loss, history of TB exposure, or a typical tree-in-bud pattern.

differential_diagnoses.name: Cavitary lung cancer (especially squamous cell carcinoma)
supporting_evidence: Case 1: A 67-year-old man with chronic hemoptysis for 2 years had a cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe, measuring approximately 4.2 cm × 5.8 cm, and had a poor response to antibacterial therapy. A solitary upper lobe cavitary lesion warrants concern for cavitary lung cancer.

Case 9: an 82-year-old man; Case 10: a 62-year-old man. Both are elderly/middle-aged to older men with persistent respiratory symptoms and abnormal imaging findings; malignancy should be included in the initial differential diagnosis.
In the image, the right upper lung lesion in Case 1 is a focal cavitary lesion; morphologically, a neoplastic cavitary lesion cannot be excluded based on the first-stage information alone.
opposing_evidence: Multiple patients had bilateral bronchiectasis, mucus plugging, aspergilloma, diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities or consolidation, etc., favoring infectious/fungal lesions rather than a uniform explanation by malignant tumors.
The phase 1 information did not provide more direct signs of malignancy such as hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, pleural indentation, or an obvious solid mass.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: [Case 1] Sputum tNGS showed: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, sequence count 80; Aspergillus fumigatus, sequence count 50; nucleic acid bacillus, sequence count 1470.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had chronic cough, sputum production, and recurrent hemoptysis for 2 years. Imaging shows a cavity in the right upper lung, and the response to cefoperazone-sulbactam combined with levofloxacin has been poor, suggesting that common bacterial infection cannot fully explain the condition and that further evaluation for special pathogens associated with cavitary lesions is needed. Sputum tNGS is suitable for simultaneous screening for bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria, and when serum G/GM, Aspergillus IgG, T-spot, and Xpert are all negative, it can compensate for the insufficient sensitivity of conventional testing and help resolve whether this cavitary lesion is due to bronchiectasis/necrotizing infection, Aspergillus infection, or mycobacterial infection, and provide a basis for whether to subsequently combine anti-Pseudomonas aeruginosa therapy, antifungal therapy, or proceed with further invasive sampling.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: 5 days later, the sputum fungal culture from our hospital returned positive for Aspergillus fumigatus.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: This patient has a right upper lobe cavitary lesion, long-term hemoptysis, and no response to antibacterial treatment. Combined with sputum tNGS that has already indicated Aspergillus fumigatus sequences, traditional etiologic methods are needed for further verification of mycologic evidence. Sputum fungal culture can help confirm whether there is Aspergillus growth in the respiratory tract and assist in distinguishing incidental molecular detection from true infection/colonization; in the setting of cavitary lesions, culture results are valuable for supporting the spectrum of chronic pulmonary aspergillosis or Aspergillus-related infection within the cavity, and can provide a basis for selecting antifungal treatment such as voriconazole.

The patient also has sputum production, cavitary lesions, and underlying bronchiectasis, and sputum tNGS indicated Pseudomonas aeruginosa; clinically, it is necessary to assess whether there is concomitant common bacterial infection or an acute exacerbation of bronchiectasis. Sputum bacterial culture is an important routine etiologic test that complements molecular testing; it can determine whether culturable bacteria are present and prepare for subsequent antimicrobial susceptibility testing and optimization of the antibacterial regimen. Even if the result is negative, it also helps indicate that common bacteria are not the predominant pathogen, thereby prompting the clinical diagnostic focus to shift toward special infections such as Aspergillus or mycobacteria.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: [Case 2] BALF-tNGS showed: Nocardia abscessus, sequence count 115; Aspergillus fumigatus, sequence count 26450.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient had recurrent hemoptysis for 1 year. He was previously considered at an outside hospital to have Nocardia infection and had received trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treatment for 1 year, but the efficacy was poor and serum creatinine increased. He was admitted again for hemoptysis. Imaging showed bronchiectasis with mucus plugging in the bilateral lower lobes, suggesting the possibility of infection with a special pathogen on the basis of chronic structural lung disease. Because the previous diagnosis needed re-evaluation, routine inflammatory markers were not elevated, and blood G/GM and Aspergillus IgG were negative, BALF-tNGS could directly perform broad screening from the lesion site for Nocardia, Aspergillus, and other difficult-to-culture pathogens, to determine whether this represented persistent Nocardia infection, coinfection with Aspergillus, or previous misdiagnosis, and would directly affect whether subsequent combined therapy targeting Nocardia and Aspergillus should be used.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: BALF bacterial culture at our hospital was negative
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: This patient has bronchiectasis, hemoptysis, and imaging findings of mucus plugging, and common bacterial infection remains one of the common causes that needs to be ruled out. BALF bacterial culture can improve the representativeness of lower respiratory tract specimens and is used to determine whether cultivable bacterial pathogens and their potential antimicrobial resistance are present; in the context of BALF-tNGS suggesting Nocardia and Aspergillus, a negative culture instead helps reduce the likelihood that ordinary bacterial bronchiectasis infection is the primary cause, helping clinicians attribute the etiology to a special infection and avoid unnecessarily escalating empiric broad-spectrum antibacterial agents.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Fungal culture was positive for Aspergillus fumigatus.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has a long disease course, recurrent hemoptysis, and imaging shows bronchiectasis and mucus plugging, and BALF-tNGS has already indicated a high sequence count of Aspergillus fumigatus; fungal culture is still needed to further confirm its clinical significance. BALF fungal culture is closer to the lesion site than sputum specimens, which helps support that Aspergillus is not merely upper airway contamination but a true infection related to the pulmonary lesion; this is very important for distinguishing Aspergillus colonization, chronic infection, and mixed infection coexisting with Nocardia, and directly affects whether to initiate or continue antifungal regimens such as voriconazole.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: BALF tNGS showed: Aspergillus fumigatus, sequence count 270; human coronavirus NL63, sequence count 47
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient had intermittent hemoptysis for 4 days. Chest CT had already shown cystic bronchiectasis in the right lower lobe, an intracavitary aspergilloma, and surrounding exudative opacities, suggesting both a preexisting structural lesion and possible concomitant active infection. Although serum G/GM and Aspergillus IgG were negative, and T-spot was positive but Xpert was negative, it remains difficult to identify the pathogen based on noninvasive testing alone. BALF tNGS can simultaneously search for multiple pathogens, including fungi and viruses, from the lesion site, to determine whether the surrounding exudative opacities are due to Aspergillus-related inflammation alone, concomitant viral infection, or other pathogens, thereby providing a basis for antifungal drug selection after hemostasis and for whether further isolation or additional treatment is needed.

Imaging in this patient has already suggested an aspergilloma and surrounding exudation, but serum GM, G test, and Aspergillus IgG were all negative, indicating that serology alone has limited sensitivity for localized or endobronchial Aspergillus lesions. BALF-GM is derived from the local lesion and can improve the ability to identify active intrapulmonary Aspergillus infection. It is mainly used to determine whether the surrounding exudation suggests Aspergillus-related invasion or active infection, rather than merely stable colonization of an aspergilloma. Its result helps strengthen the diagnostic evidence for Aspergillus, supports initiation of systemic antifungal therapy, and together with BALF-tNGS and culture results improves diagnostic confidence.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: [Case 5] BALF-tNGS showed: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, sequence count 16112; Moraxella catarrhalis, sequence count 170. BALF culture at our hospital showed mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had recurrent cough and sputum production for more than 30 years, with worsening over the past 4 months. CT showed bilateral bronchiectasis with infection, placing the patient in a high-risk population for recurrent infection in chronic structural lung disease. Although procalcitonin was negative and serum fungal and TB-related tests were negative, the most important clinical question is whether there is bronchiectasis-related bacterial colonization/infection, especially with important pathogens such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa that affect prognosis and medication selection. BALF culture can directly obtain higher-quality specimens from the lower airways, determine whether the Pseudomonas aeruginosa indicated by molecular testing is a true pathogen, and provide key evidence for antimicrobial selection, treatment duration, and whether coverage for drug-resistant/mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa is needed.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: One month later, BALF mycobacterial culture at our hospital showed Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is 18 years old, with 2 months of cough, sputum production, and blood-streaked sputum. Imaging showed bronchiectasis with infection, and the patient's diabetes had been very poorly controlled in the past, constituting a susceptible background for infections such as TB. Although the initial Xpert was negative, the patient had no sputum and had already undergone bronchoscopy, BALF-tNGS indicated a high sequence count for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, so further confirmation is still required using culture, a traditional gold-standard-level method. BALF mycobacterial culture can determine whether the molecular detection represents true active TB infection, and provide a basis for subsequent species identification, drug resistance assessment, and standardized anti-TB treatment; it is decisive for excluding a purely bacterial infection associated with bronchiectasis.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Both BALF-Xpert and mycobacterial culture at our hospital were positive.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient had recurrent cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea for more than 1 year, with worsening for 3 days. Cephalosporin treatment was ineffective. Imaging showed bilateral bronchiectasis with inflammation; meanwhile, T-spot was positive, and BALF-tNGS suggested Nocardia, but TB still could not be excluded. BALF-Xpert can rapidly detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis and assess rifampin resistance-related information in lower respiratory tract specimens obtained by bronchoscopy, addressing the question of whether TB is also present when there is evidence suggesting Nocardia infection. This test has a direct role in establishing an early diagnosis of mixed infection, avoiding missed diagnosis of TB, guiding isolation, and initiating anti-TB treatment, and it can also explain the poor response to antibacterial treatment alone.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: At our hospital, CMV, EBV, and PCP nucleic acid tests were positive.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is 82 years old and has been taking oral glucocorticoids long-term for ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis. Recently, dyspnea has worsened. CT showed bilateral reticular and ground-glass opacities, interlobular septal thickening, and traction bronchiectasis, indicating marked immunosuppression and a high-risk population for opportunistic infections. Previously, the G test was elevated, while GM, T-spot, and Xpert were negative. Sputum tNGS also suggested multiple pathogens including PCP, Candida, CMV, and EBV, making it necessary to further confirm whether CMV is truly involved in the pulmonary lesions. CMV nucleic acid testing is used to determine evidence of cytomegalovirus replication, helps distinguish bystander activation from CMV pneumonia, and is of important significance for whether to initiate ganciclovir and for prognostic assessment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: At our hospital, CMV, EBV, and PCP nucleic acid tests were positive.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: In this patient, diffuse ground-glass opacities and dyspnea developed in the setting of long-term steroid-induced immunosuppression. Sputum tNGS indicated a high EBV sequence burden, but EBV may be detected in respiratory specimens due to reactivation or as a bystander finding, and its clinical significance requires further confirmation. The purpose of EBV nucleic acid testing is to assess whether viral reactivation is present and to determine the viral load level, to help judge whether EBV is related to the current pulmonary inflammation or is merely a bystander in the setting of immunosuppression. This test helps refine the assessment of the spectrum of opportunistic infections and avoid treating all molecular detections as pathogenic, thereby allowing a more rational focus of treatment priorities.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: At our hospital, CMV, EBV, and PCP nucleic acid tests were positive.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has been receiving long-term glucocorticoid therapy and has had recent worsening dyspnea. Imaging shows diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities and septal thickening, which represent a typical high-risk background and one of the common imaging patterns of Pneumocystis pneumonia. At the same time, an elevated G test also supports the possibility of fungal infection/PCP. Although sputum tNGS suggests PCP sequences, further targeted nucleic acid testing is needed to increase diagnostic specificity and determine whether this represents true Pneumocystis infection rather than simple colonization. This test is directly related to whether to initiate trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treatment as early as possible, whether combined management of mixed opportunistic infections such as CMV is needed, and helps clarify whether the diffuse interstitial lung disease reflects infection or exacerbation of the underlying lung disease.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text:
[Case 1] Sputum tNGS showed: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, sequence count 80; Aspergillus fumigatus, sequence count 50; Fusobacterium nucleatum, sequence count 1470. Five days later, sputum fungal culture at our hospital reported Aspergillus fumigatus. Sputum bacterial culture (-).
[Case 2] BALF-tNGS showed: Nocardia abscessus, sequence count 115; Aspergillus fumigatus, sequence count 26450. BALF bacterial culture at our hospital was negative, and fungal culture showed Aspergillus fumigatus.
[Case 3] Sputum tNGS showed: Fusobacterium nucleatum, sequence count 748; Streptococcus anginosus group, sequence count 88; Human coronavirus NL63, sequence count 36344; Herpes simplex virus type I, sequence count 20. Alveolar lavage fluid tNGS showed: Aspergillus fumigatus, sequence count 270; Human coronavirus NL63, sequence count 47. BALF-GM assay: 1.52, BALF fungal culture (-).
[Case 4] Sputum tNGS showed: Aspergillus fumigatus, sequence count 4027; Aspergillus terreus complex, sequence count 1496; Rhizopus microsporus, sequence count 11; Candida albicans, sequence count 496; Human adenovirus group B, sequence count 27447.
[Case 5] BALF-tNGS showed: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, sequence count 16112; Moraxella catarrhalis, sequence count 170. BALF culture at our hospital showed mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
[Case 6] BALF-tNGS showed: Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, sequence count 59028; Mycoplasma genus, sequence count 12; Klebsiella pneumoniae, sequence count 762; Bordetella pertussis, sequence count 21. One month later, BALF mycobacterial culture at our hospital showed Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
[Case 7] BALF-tNGS showed: Nocardia cyriacigeorgica, sequence count 14224; Rhinovirus C, sequence count 37866. BALF-Xpert and mycobacterial culture at our hospital were both positive.
[Case 8] BALF-tNGS showed: Influenza A virus H1N1, sequence count 6382; Cytomegalovirus, sequence count 2119; Epstein-Barr virus, sequence count 83.
[Case 9] Sputum tNGS showed: Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCP), sequence count 2125; Candida tropicalis, sequence count 12076; Candida albicans, sequence count 32961; Herpes simplex virus type I, sequence count 112; CMV, sequence count 90; EBV, sequence count 6239. Testing at our hospital showed positive nucleic acid results for CMV, EBV, and PCP. Two weeks later, repeat sputum tNGS showed: Rhizopus oryzae, sequence count 362; Candida tropicalis, sequence count 20909; Candida albicans, sequence count 43028; CMV, sequence count 141. During the subsequent hospitalization, sputum tNGS showed: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, sequence count 951, macrolide resistance; Candida krusei, sequence count 233391; Candida tropicalis, sequence count 10957; Candida albicans, sequence count 17185.
[Case 10] Sputum tNGS showed: Klebsiella pneumoniae, sequence count 122; Escherichia coli, sequence count 90; Acinetobacter baumannii, sequence count 1281; Rhizopus microsporus, sequence count 705; Pneumocystis jirovecii, sequence count 703; EBV, sequence count 6584.
